notes: Answers were written by reading src/requests directly and confirming each fact against the source, not by running either system; verifying them caught two errors in my own first draft. Locations are the code that genuinely answers the question — for a 'what calls X' question, the call sites rather than the definition of X. Questions with `accept_any` have one answer that several locations evidence equally well, so finding any one is full credit; without it the question asks for an enumeration and every location is a separate item. That distinction follows the wording of the question and was fixed before the scored run, after a smoke test showed the graph systems being marked down for naming a callee's definition where a text chunk happened to cover the call site.

questions.question: Which classes inherit directly from RequestException?
questions.answer: Fifteen classes list RequestException as a direct base, all in src/requests/exceptions.py: InvalidJSONError, HTTPError, ConnectionError, Timeout, URLRequired, TooManyRedirects, MissingSchema, InvalidSchema, InvalidURL, InvalidHeader, ChunkedEncodingError, ContentDecodingError, StreamConsumedError, RetryError and UnrewindableBodyError. Several of them have a second base as well (ValueError, TypeError, BaseHTTPError).
questions.notes: Deliberately says 'directly': ProxyError, SSLError, ConnectTimeout, ReadTimeout, InvalidProxyURL and JSONDecodeError inherit from RequestException only transitively.

questions.question: What does requests.api.get call?
questions.answer: requests.api.get calls requests.api.request, passing the method name "get" along with the url and any keyword arguments.
questions.notes: Two equally valid pieces of evidence: get's own body, where the call appears, or the definition of the callee it names. A graph traversal naturally surfaces the second, a text chunk the first.

questions.question: What calls the function _basic_auth_str?
questions.answer: _basic_auth_str is called from four places: HTTPBasicAuth.__call__ and HTTPProxyAuth.__call__ in auth.py, HTTPAdapter.proxy_headers in adapters.py, and SessionRedirectMixin.rebuild_proxies in sessions.py. The first sets the Authorization header; the other three set Proxy-Authorization.

questions.question: Which class does HTTPProxyAuth inherit from?
questions.answer: HTTPProxyAuth inherits from HTTPBasicAuth. It overrides __call__ to set the Proxy-Authorization header instead of Authorization.

questions.question: Which classes does PreparedRequest inherit from?
questions.answer: PreparedRequest inherits from two mixins, RequestEncodingMixin and RequestHooksMixin, both defined in models.py.

questions.question: What functions are defined in the hooks module?
questions.answer: hooks.py defines two functions: default_hooks, which returns a dict mapping each event name to an empty list, and dispatch_hook, which runs a hook dictionary against a piece of data.

questions.question: What methods does the HTTPDigestAuth class define?
questions.answer: HTTPDigestAuth defines six methods: __init__, init_per_thread_state, build_digest_header, handle_redirect, handle_401 and __call__. Unlike HTTPBasicAuth it does not define __eq__ or __ne__.
questions.notes: build_digest_header contains several nested hash helpers (md5_utf8, sha_utf8, sha256_utf8, sha512_utf8, KD); those are inner functions, not methods of the class.

questions.question: Where is dispatch_hook called from?
questions.answer: dispatch_hook is called once, from Session.send in sessions.py, which dispatches the "response" hook over the response before returning it.

questions.question: When requests follows a redirect, which method decides whether to drop the Authorization header, and what does it compare?
questions.answer: SessionRedirectMixin.should_strip_auth makes the decision, and rebuild_auth calls it. It compares the old and new URL: a different hostname always strips the header, and otherwise a changed port or changed scheme strips it. There is one deliberate exception — an http to https redirect on the standard ports (80 to 443) keeps the header, for backwards compatibility.

questions.question: Which HTTP status codes cause requests to change the request method when following a redirect, and what does it change the method to?
questions.answer: SessionRedirectMixin.rebuild_method changes the method to GET in three cases: 303 See Other for any method except HEAD, 302 Found for any method except HEAD, and 301 Moved Permanently when the original method was POST.

questions.question: Which method picks the transport adapter for a URL, and how do adapters get registered in the first place?
questions.answer: Session.get_adapter selects an adapter by matching the URL against the registered prefixes, and raises InvalidSchema if none matches. Adapters are registered by Session.mount, which stores the adapter under a prefix and keeps the mapping sorted so that longer, more specific prefixes are matched first.

questions.question: How does a redirect response get turned into the next request URL?
questions.answer: SessionRedirectMixin.get_redirect_target reads the Location header from a redirect response and returns it as a native string, or None when the response is not a redirect. resolve_redirects then uses that target, resolving relative URLs against the previous request and looping while further redirects are returned.

questions.question: Which function builds the Basic auth header value, and which helper does it use to turn the encoded credentials into a string?
questions.answer: _basic_auth_str in auth.py builds the header value. It base64-encodes the username and password and passes the result through to_native_string, from _internal_utils, to produce the final "Basic ..." string.

questions.question: PreparedRequest has several prepare_* methods. Which one sets the request method, and what does it do to the value?
questions.answer: PreparedRequest.prepare_method sets self.method, upper-casing it and converting it to a native string with to_native_string when it is not None.

questions.question: Where is SSL certificate verification handled?
questions.answer: HTTPAdapter.cert_verify in adapters.py handles it. It decides whether verification is on, picks the CA bundle (the default one or a user-supplied path), sets cert_reqs and ca_certs/ca_cert_dir on the urllib3 connection, and applies any client-side certificate given via the cert argument.

questions.question: How does requests convert a value that might be bytes into a string, and what encoding does it assume?
questions.answer: to_native_string in _internal_utils.py does this. It returns str input unchanged and decodes bytes input, assuming ASCII unless a different encoding is passed.

questions.question: How does requests check whether a string contains only ASCII characters?
questions.answer: unicode_is_ascii in _internal_utils.py tries to encode the string as ASCII and returns True if that succeeds, or False if it raises UnicodeEncodeError.

questions.question: What data structure does requests use so that HTTP header lookups ignore case, and how does it compare two of them for equality?
questions.answer: CaseInsensitiveDict in structures.py. It stores each entry keyed by the lower-cased header name while remembering the original casing, and its __eq__ compares two mappings by their lower-cased items, so case differences do not affect equality.

questions.question: How is the default set of hooks for a request created, and what does it contain?
questions.answer: default_hooks in hooks.py builds it, returning a dictionary with one key for each name in HOOKS mapped to an empty list. In practice HOOKS contains only "response", so a fresh request starts with {"response": []}.

questions.question: Where does requests decide how many redirects are too many, and what does it raise?
questions.answer: SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects counts redirects and raises TooManyRedirects when the count exceeds the session's max_redirects, which defaults to DEFAULT_REDIRECT_LIMIT.

questions.question: What happens to the Proxy-Authorization header when a request is redirected?
questions.answer: SessionRedirectMixin.rebuild_proxies handles it. It unconditionally deletes any existing Proxy-Authorization header, then sets a fresh one via _basic_auth_str only when the new URL's proxy carries credentials and the scheme is not https — the header is deliberately withheld from TLS-tunnelled requests, where it could leak.

questions.question: How does requests attach Basic authentication credentials to an outgoing request?
questions.answer: HTTPBasicAuth is a callable auth object: its __call__ receives the PreparedRequest and sets the Authorization header to the value returned by _basic_auth_str, then returns the request.
